📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced Yorkers got a space-y surprise on Wednesday (Nov. 11): Retired NASA astronaut and U.S. Navy Captain Sunita "Suni" Williams rolled down 5th Avenue in the back of a classic convertible wrapped in patriotic decals as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade.

On Wednesday, Fresh York City's 107th annual Veterans Day Parade made its way through Manhattan to the cheers and respectful nods of thousands of onlookers.

The parade is an annual tradition on the holiday, which honors veterans of the U.S. armed forces. As part of the parade, veterans, active-duty soldiers, firefighters, marching bands, youth cadets and more march through the city and honor those who have served and sacrificed in the U.S. military.

Recent findings suggest that this year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join Newly introduced Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event.

Industry observers note that williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025. She spent 608 days in space during her astronaut career, the second-most by an American astronaut behind Peggy Whitson, who racked up 695.

It has been revealed that williams also had an extensive career in the U.S. Navy. She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017.

Industry observers note that during this time, Williams supported relief efforts following Hurricane Andrew, trained within the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and gained a wealth of further experience flying as a military pilot.

Williams is part of a longstanding tradition of astronauts serving in the U.S. military. From test pilots to naval officers and more, there's a strong link between the U.S. armed forces and NASA's astronaut program.

It has been revealed that chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shania Twain is standing up for others in country music.
  • The legendary star in the genre used her acceptance speech for the Equal Play Award at Sunday’s CMT Awards to call for more equity and diversity in the country music industry.
  • “When I wrote the phrase ‘Man I feel like a woman’ I honestly had no idea at the time it would become an undercurrent of a decades-long career,” she noted, referring to one of her biggest hits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shania Twain is standing up for others in country music.

The legendary star in the genre used her acceptance speech for the Equal Play Award at Sunday’s CMT Awards to call for more equity and diversity in the country music industry.

“When I wrote the phrase ‘Man I feel like a woman’ I honestly had no idea at the time it would become an undercurrent of a decades-long career,” she noted, referring to one of her biggest hits. “It’s amazing how one statement can empower so many.”.

The phrase, Twain said, “has been adopted by an array of fantastic communities all around the world and become a genuine path of power…which brings me so much joy.”.

In a recent development, “I believe in an all-inclusive country music. We’re family,” Twain stated. “This is a genre of music with a rich history that raised and nurtured my own songwriting and performance and recording career from childhood. Presently, the industry standard does a real disservice to this.”.

Twain, who was presented the award by rapper Megan Thee Stallion, shouted out some of the diverse acts she is spotlighting on her “Queen of Me” tour this year, including Lily Rose, Lindsay Ell, Hailey Whitters, Mickey Guyton and others.

“I will continue to do my best as a trailblazer,” Twain noted. “Together, let’s ensure all our fellow artists get equal play regardless of gender, age or race.”.

Industry observers note that she also performed acappella with the African American singing group, The BoykinZ, while presenting an award onstage. Twain connected with the group, who are sisters and rising country stars, after Kelly Clarkson surprised them recently by bringing Twain out to meet them during an episode of Clarkson’s daytime talk show.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw.
  • In a recent development, sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury.
  • Industry observers note that manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw.

In a recent development, sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager stated the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. Suzanne Wrack.

Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City.

Industry observers note that manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace. Maya Le Tissier stole the headlines with her goal on her 150th appearance for the club but the team’s improved defensive stability is also catching the eye and the centre-back is key to that. “For a defender you expect as the minimum you need to defend well and help to build,” stated the head coach, Eva Olid. “But now she’s scoring goals and that is more than a manager can ask from a centre-back. She’s in a high level and I’m so happy for her.” Le Tissier is showing consistent solidity and appears to be enjoying life under Olid now that things have settled, after seven goals conceded in their opening two WSL games. United have conceded four in eight WSL games since and are starting to show their flair. SW.

Industry observers note that have teams stopped fearing Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium? Their run of five consecutive WSL draws at home suggests so. London City Lionesses had 56% possession on Sunday and controlled the game for significant spells, especially in the second half, and although Arsenal created the greater chances, they do not play with the aura of a side attracting the largest attendances in the division. Renée Slegers was asked whether she was worried her team were losing that home “fear factor” and noted: “No, because we love playing at the Emirates. We had the biggest crowd so far in the season, the atmosphere was fantastic under the lights.” Probed further about her side’s home form, the head coach said: “I don’t think we’ve lost the fear factor, I think it’s a very hard place for oppositions to come.” Her side host West Ham next Sunday, looking for that elusive home WSL win. Tom Garry.

Match report: Arsenal 1-1 London City.

Sources indicate that tottenham Hotspur were the latest team frustrated by Everton’s defensive solidity as they were held to a goalless draw. Despite controlling the ball and registering 17 shots, only three efforts were on target as they failed to score for the first time. Martin Ho was keen to highlight their opponents’ strengths as a key reason. “When we got into that attacking third, it was going to take something really special,” he told Spursplay. “They defended so deep with so many numbers behind the ball. You’re waiting for one of those moments to drop.” It was just the kind of performance fans have come to expect from Scott Phelan’s side. Unbeaten in their past three, in which they have faced Manchester United, Chelsea and Spurs, Everton have developed a strong resilience and character in recent weeks. Where they struggle is at the other end. Everton have scored eight goals this season (three of them own goals), higher than only Charlton in the WSL. Sophie Downey.

Liverpool ended their five-game winless league run with a statement victory over struggling Brighton, their third away win in 17 games. It has been a frustrating October and November block for Gareth Taylor and his team so there was much relief on the sideline that they were finally able to turn performance and opportunity into three points. Liverpool had less of the ball but their fast counterattacking proved too much for the Seagulls. A significant key to their success was Beata Olsson. She has six goals from her past five games in all competitions, stepping up when her team have needed it most. Injuries have kept out Aurélie Csillag and Ceri Holland for the best part of the season and Sophie Roman Haug is recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury sustained 13 months ago. With limited attacking options, therefore, it will be very welcome that the Swedish striker has found her form in front of goal. SD.

In a recent development, viviane Asseyi continued her impressive scoring form with a superb brace in West Ham’s 2-0 victory over Charlton, taking her WSL tally to seven this season. The striker opened the scoring with a composed finish from the edge of the area before producing the standout moment of the afternoon, curling a spectacular 25-yard free-kick into the top corner beyond Charlton’s goalkeeper, Anna Koivunen. Asseyi could have completed a hat-trick but her two goals proved decisive. West Ham’s head coach, Rita Guarino, described her as “an notable player”, adding that Asseyi was in a good goalscoring spell. Guarino felt Asseyi could have been happier with a hat-trick, but her latest double underlines her importance to West Ham’s attacking threat. Mitul Samji.

Poor officiating dominated the narrative of the second city derby as Aston Villa edged Birmingham City 1-0, with both sides feeling hard done by. First, City felt Lucy Parker had fouled Océane Hurtré in the penalty area in the 24th minute, only for the referee to award a corner. Whether the incident was inside the box was disputable, but it did appear to be a foul. Minutes later, Villa had a goal from Océane Deslandes overruled for what was declared a foul on the goalkeeper in another contentious call, but they managed to find a winner in the second half. The decisions added to growing concerns about consistency in the WSL. Ho recently suggested officiating had worsened, and matches such as this do little to ease those concerns. Before VAR is introduced, improving the quality of refereeing must be a priority to avoid undermining the league’s standards and progress. Réshma Rao.

TL;DR: Hasbro's $39.97 Blooms by Play-Doh Rose Bouquet Kit lets adults craft 20 display-ready faux roses with baby's breath. It debuted exclusively at Walmart on Nov. 13, before expanding to other retailers in early 2027.

Recent findings suggest that play-Doh is officially getting into home decor. With the launch of the Blooms by Play-Doh Rose Bouquet Kit, the brand has expanded its adult crafting lineup to offer a hands-on project with a display-worthy payoff: a complete, permanent vase of red roses and baby's breath made entirely by hand.

Sources indicate that designed for crafters of all skill levels, the all-in-one box packs everything you need to build an arrangement of 20 bold red roses accented with sprigs of baby's breath. Instead of fiddling with florist wire or messy hot glue, the set comes loaded with Play-Doh compound, flower-making extruder tools, faux greenery, a vase, and step-by-step instructions.

You simply use the blooming tool to press and shape the petals into full blossoms, let the compound dry, mist them with finishing spray to lock everything in place, and arrange the bouquet in the included vase.

Sources indicate that once everything dries, you have a solid, display-ready centerpiece that will not droop after three days on your table. It is an easy, low-maintenance craft whether you are putting it together for a party or just want a relaxing creative project that does not involve a screen.

You can pick up the Blooms by Play-Doh Rose Bouquet Kit now for $39.97 exclusively at Walmart. If you are eyeing one for holiday gifting, Walmart holds the exclusive run through the season before it arrives at other retailers in early 2027.

#13075. I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1958 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a great model to learn the basics of manual telescope operation and get great views of your chosen targets, thanks to intuitive smartphone integration, but it isn't as easy to set up as you might think.
  • Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a great model to learn the basics of manual telescope operation and get great views of your chosen targets, thanks to intuitive smartphone integration, but it isn't as easy to set up as you might think.

Sharp, high-contrast 150mm optics.

Difficult and heavy to lift and move.

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a new telescope.

Industry observers note that finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit.

Industry observers note that it was a stunning view, and exactly the kind of experience a beginner needs from a first telescope. There was no frustration and no wondering whether I was looking in the right place. StarSense took me straight there — but, crucially, I moved the telescope myself. I’ve always liked that combination of hand-holding and DIY observing that Celestron’s StarSense tech gives you.

I’m less convinced by the tabletop telescope it’s attached to. Although this $599 RRP (£379) model is significantly smaller than the Celestron StarSense Explorer 8-inch Dobsonian telescope I’ve previously reviewed, it still weighs 25 lbs (11.33 kg). You need to place it on something sturdy before you can use it comfortably. After living with it in my backyard, I’m not convinced the tabletop format is the advantage it initially appears to be.

In a recent development, I’ve used Celestron’s StarSense Explorer system on a variety of telescopes and have always been impressed by how easy this type of smartphone navigation is to use. The technology works just as well here and, for me, it remains one of the best ways of making a traditional optical telescope accessible to a complete beginner.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t a computerized GoTo telescope. There are no motors to slew across the sky automatically and no tracking system to keep an object centered. Instead, a smartphone sits in a dock attached to the telescope, and its camera looks at the sky via a small mirror. Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app analyzes the reflections of the stars it sees, works out exactly where the telescope is pointing and tells you which direction to push it to reach the object you want to observe.

My iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted perfectly into the dock, and the initial alignment process was identical to what I’d used before. Once that was done, I used StarSense to find the Pleiades (M45), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Double Cluster in Perseus and Saturn. It worked every time, with the target appearing in the eyepiece when the app told me I had reached it.

I can find all of those objects without an app, but that’s not really the point. Beginners often struggle to translate a star chart or an astronomy app into actual telescope movements. StarSense gives you confidence that you’re heading in the right direction while still requiring you to operate it physically.

That makes it a useful way to learn the night sky. After repeatedly pushing the telescope from one familiar object to another, you begin to understand how everything fits together. That’s very different from pressing a button and watching a GoTo or smart telescope move itself, and it’s why I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, even on a relatively wide-field telescope like this one.

In a recent development, the StarSense system may be the headline feature, but the reason to buy any Dobsonian is aperture. This one uses a 150mm (5.9-inch) parabolic primary mirror with a 750mm focal length and a relatively fast f/5 focal ratio. That combination gives it fairly low-power, wide-field views that are particularly well suited to large star clusters.

The Pleiades was one of my favorite views. At 30x through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, the telescope gave me a sharp field of stars and a particularly good view of what I call “Carter’s Whip” — the curving line of stars running through the cluster. I saw little obvious softness towards the edges, and focusing was straightforward.

Industry observers note that the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) was a different proposition. From my light-polluted backyard, I could see Andromeda’s bright core, but not its outskirts or its satellite galaxies. That’s largely a consequence of observing a galaxy from a city, not a criticism of a 150mm telescope, but it’s a useful reminder of what visual astronomy is actually like. Don’t expect the colorful, detailed views of galaxies and nebulas you see in astrophotos, such as the stacked images a smart telescope can give you.

Saturn was more rewarding, but I would have liked more magnification when the seeing was this good. Add a Barlow lens if planets are a priority — it can double the magnification of any eyepiece you use it with.

Industry observers note that overall, I was impressed by the telescope’s optics. The views were sharp and contrast-y, and there’s enough aperture here to make a serious start in visual astronomy. However, the two supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces are decidedly entry-level — and obvious candidates for upgrading in the medium term.

The focuser is a weak point. It’s a fairly basic 1.25-inch rack-and-pinion design, but I noticed some wobble and vibration while using it. That’s a shame because the focuser is one of the parts of a telescope you constantly interact with, and something smoother and more precise would make the entire instrument feel more accomplished.

In a recent development, the tabletop design isn’t necessarily as convenient as it sounds. I expected this scope to feel considerably more convenient than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Dobsonian. The base has built-in grab handles, but the assembled telescope's shape and weight make it awkward to lift onto a table — I certainly wouldn’t recommend it to anyone with a bad back. You could move the optical tube and base separately, but that starts to cancel out the convenience of owning a relatively compact tabletop telescope.

You also need to choose your table carefully. It has to be sturdy enough not to introduce vibrations, but not so large that you have to stretch across it to reach the eyepiece as the telescope points to different parts of the sky. I found myself bending and stretching into some awkward positions.

Once it’s in position, the Dobsonian mount worked well. The balance was good, and I didn't need to adjust the altitude tension, while the movements offered a useful mix of resistance and fluidity as I followed StarSense around the sky. At 75x, however, keeping Saturn centered was more difficult than I expected. It was easy to over-nudge the telescope, then correct in the opposite direction.

Sources indicate that celestron sells an optional tripod for the telescope, and after using the tabletop base, I can see why that might be attractive. However, I’d personally rather put the money towards a larger Dobsonian whose base is designed to sit directly on the ground.

This scope doesn’t arrive in one piece. Assembly took about 90 minutes, and it required all manner of screws and screwdrivers. The main problem was getting the screws into the holes in the Dobsonian base, which took so much effort that I ended up with a blister on my hand. That’s not what I expected from a telescope aimed at beginners, especially when almost everything about using it has been designed to make things easy.

Once built, things improved considerably. My review sample arrived well collimated, so I didn’t have to adjust the mirror alignment. The tube rings, phone dock and general construction were all good enough for a telescope at this price, and nothing about the telescope felt particularly fragile. Once the telescope is outside, on a suitable table and aligned, it’s an impressively straightforward instrument to use.

It has been revealed that the more I used the StarSense Explorer 150mm Dobsonian, the more I wondered who really benefits from the tabletop format. It’s certainly smaller than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Explorer Dobsonian, but it’s still a substantial object to store, and I didn’t feel any more inclined to grab it for a quick observing session.

Recent findings suggest that going bigger offers an optical advantage. An 8-inch/203mm aperture collects about 83% more light than a 150mm aperture, which matters when you’re observing faint deep-sky objects. The 8-inch StarSense also had a much nicer 2-inch Crayford focuser, and generally felt like a telescope with a little more room to grow into.

According to recent reports, dobsonians are the perfect companion to smart telescopes. The latter have completely changed what beginners can photograph from their backyards, particularly under light pollution. They can reveal galaxies and nebulas that are extremely difficult or impossible to see visually. I use them all the time. But they are no substitute for navigating to and actually seeing objects in the night sky with your own eyes.

Industry observers note that the two approaches don’t need to compete. A smart telescope has to be pointed and then left alone for an hour or four to stack images. That time could be spent pushing something like the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian around the sky, and actually looking through an eyepiece at the same objects. One reveals you far more than your eyes can detect, but the other lets you see the photons yourself — and make a human connection with the night sky.

At $599 RRP (£379), the StarSense Explorer 150mm sits in an interesting part of the beginner telescope market. There are smaller tabletop Dobsonians like the Celestron Moon Mission 100mm without smartphone navigation, but I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, particularly for a first-time telescope owner.

If you mainly want to observe planets and the moon, a refractor like the Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ also makes sense. However, if you want to go relatively large, I do recommend the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian — with an notable qualification. Its optics are good, StarSense is superb, and it’s an excellent way for a beginner to learn their way around the night sky, but I’m not convinced that 150mm is the sweet spot for this particular design. It’s too massive to feel genuinely convenient as a tabletop telescope, yet not big enough to deliver the full advantages of a larger Dobsonian.

If space is tight, this is a very capable first telescope. If you have room for the 8-inch StarSense Explorer, I’d go bigger.

Sources indicate that jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

Are Scotland still too reliant on 'old guard'?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the captain's record-breaking 103rd cap played out in cruel fashion.
  • In a recent development, so too were John McGinn and Kieran Tierney.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scotland slump to 4-0 defeat in Switzerland.

As Zeki Amdouni arrowed in second-string Switzerland's fabulous fourth goal, the body language of dejected Scotland duo Andy Robertson and Ryan Christie was telling.

Recent findings suggest that the captain's record-breaking 103rd cap played out in cruel fashion. Suited and booted for the occasion, with commemorative boots and a personalised armband, there was no cause for celebration as Robertson was, yet again, wheeled out afterwards to make sense of the 4-0 scudding in St Gallen.

In a recent development, so too were John McGinn and Kieran Tierney. Billy Gilmour, who has also surpassed the half-century caps landmark, also did a bit of talking. Substitute Christie was spared this time.

After a result of this kind, rounding up a humdrum maiden campaign for manager Sebastien Pocognoli, it's necessary for the experienced heads to front-up.

When he named his first squad, so much kudos was thrown the Belgian's way for breaking away from the norm and bleeding in the stars of tomorrow.

But such young and bright lights were only allowed to shine on the bench, at best, as Pocognoli turned to the tried and tested.

As former Scotland international Leanne Crichton remarked on BBC Scotland's Sportscene: "There's a reliance still, clearly, on that key core of Scotland players.

According to recent reports, "And, when you listen to it post-match, they sound dejected, they don't sound that confident about what is going on. It is a difficult place to be.".

Pocognoli's abject Scotland suffer 4-0 Nations League defeat in Switzerland.

St Gallen was a mighty troubling place for the Scots on Monday night.

The calm, picturesque city was invaded by coral shirt and kilt-clad Scotsmen from Sunday, but they - and their heroes on the pitch - couldn't wait to get out of the place after a poor showing at the Sitterstadion.

A narrow half-time deficit turned into a drubbing on the final whistle, at which the Scots remained goalless despite a handful of hopeful situations.

McGinn, the scorer of Scotland's past three goals, directed a weak header goalbound before the break, while Scott McTominay - nearly one year on from his Hampden heroics against Denmark - missed a couple of glaring opportunities.

"If McTominay is not operating at his highest level for the national team, there is an impact on results," Crichton said.

"If McGinn doesn't produce the goods on an evening, we're in trouble.

"If Gilmour and Ferguson in the middle of the pitch [don't perform], if Christie doesn't come on with an impact, we are [too reliant].

"And that's where you need to breed a different confidence in a different group.".

Kieron Bowie, who many hoped would be in from the off, came on just before the hour mark and got right in about it, as is the striker's style.

Winger Ben Gannon-Doak, dropped for Aaron Hickey, did come on after the wing-back ended up going off with an apparent hamstring injury before Kristi Montgomery was handed a debut with five minutes to go.

Recent findings suggest that wide-men Findlay Curtis and Josh McPake were left on the bench, again. Robbie Ure didn't make either matchday squad this camp.

All three natural wingers excite supporters, even if they have only been handed a matter of minutes, but Pocognoli's system does not suit them.

That said, the players insist they're invested in the project.

"We have to believe that we're going in the right direction," Robertson added after a beyond-deflating defeat.

"Of course, there's going to be humps in the road, but when I look back on Steve Clarke's opening six games - I can't remember all the results but - I don't think everyone was shouting and screaming about Steve Clarke's Scotland after the first six games.

"We're trying to get a team together and we're trying to build a good atmosphere off the pitch.

Recent findings suggest that "People wanted change within the squad. We've done that change and now we need to try and integrate the squad.

"We need to get close as a squad again, integrate the young players, make them feel a part of it, make them step up - it's for us to try and help them do it.".

What's the story with Pocognoli, is it now time to go?

Pocognoli wants patience but Scotland 'don't have time' says Robertson.

Breaking: A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory.
  • In a recent development, unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes.
  • A upcoming study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory. However, latest research suggests that the success of such a mission could depend heavily on which side of the asteroid receives the blast.

In a recent development, unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes. Those differences can dramatically influence how an asteroid moves when exposed to intense radiation.

A upcoming study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid. In one simulation, the asteroid's speed changed by 3.9 millimeters per second when irradiated from one direction, compared with only 0.8 millimeters per second from another. That represents a nearly fivefold difference in deflection velocity, the change in the asteroid's forward speed caused by the burst.

According to recent reports, "We expected aim to matter," noted Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories who led the research. "What surprised us was how much.".

Sources indicate that the effects on an asteroid's rotation could be even more dramatic. For another simulated asteroid, the change in how quickly it spun varied by a factor of 17 depending on the direction of the X-rays.

These findings suggest that understanding an asteroid's shape and carefully selecting where to direct a nuclear blast could be essential to protecting Earth from a future impact.

The research received funding through Sandia's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program.

A Latest Way to Simulate Asteroid Deflection.

To investigate how different asteroid shapes respond to nuclear blasts, Moore and his colleagues developed what they describe as the most accurate asteroid deflection model yet.

According to recent reports, earlier computer models faced a major limitation. Researchers typically had to choose between representing an asteroid's complex shape and performing highly detailed calculations of the physical forces involved. Combining both approaches demanded more computing power than was practical.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced system overcomes that obstacle, allowing scientists to study realistic asteroid shapes while maintaining the precision needed to calculate their response to an X-ray burst. The result is the most detailed simulation of asteroid deflection produced so far.

In a recent development, "Our upcoming algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough," Moore said. "With the old models, computers just couldn't handle it.".

Why Lumpy Asteroids Change Everything.

It has been revealed that moore's interest in improving these calculations grew out of an earlier experiment using Sandia's Z machine. That experiment provided the first demonstration that X-rays could deflect a small piece of asteroid material.

The next challenge was determining how the same physical process might affect an entire asteroid.

"I started wondering how to scale up the calculation to more accurately predict deflection of a full-scale asteroid.".

It has been revealed that A major problem was the widespread practice of treating asteroids as spheres. Although this simplifies the mathematics, it overlooks the irregular shapes of real asteroids, which can have ridges, depressions, and uneven surfaces.

"You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes," he noted. "That's when I latched onto some work one of my colleagues was doing related to outgassing of objects in space. I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this. No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid.".

The solution involved bringing together two sophisticated simulation systems already used at Sandia for very different types of physical problems.

"The ALEGRA code is normally used to model fast, high-energy experiments, like magnetically imploding wires on the Z machine, while SPARTA, a direct simulation Monte Carlo code, is usually used to model comparatively weak, slowly evolving forces, like the drag on a satellite from the solar wind," Moore explained.

"The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches.".

Predicting What Happens After a Nuclear Blast.

Sources indicate that the latest computer model allows researchers to reconstruct an asteroid using detailed 3D images captured during spacecraft flybys. They can then simulate a nuclear X-ray burst while adjusting the explosion's strength, its distance from the asteroid, and the direction from which the radiation arrives.

Industry observers note that the software calculates how much material would vaporize across different parts of the asteroid's surface and displays the results as a heat map. Using that information, it estimates the resulting push, changes in the asteroid's rotation, and the extent of surface damage.

These calculations are important because a successful planetary defense mission would ideally change an asteroid's trajectory without breaking it into multiple dangerous fragments. Redirecting one large object could be preferable to creating several pieces that might still threaten Earth.

However, the simulations cannot yet predict every possible consequence of a nuclear blast.

It has been revealed that "Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We can't predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore noted.

Developing that capability will require additional research, investment, and more advanced computational tools. An intense X-ray burst can trigger numerous physical effects, some of which influence one another. Accounting for all those interactions makes it exceptionally difficult to predict exactly how an asteroid would behave during a real deflection attempt.

Choosing the Right Blast Could Save Earth.

Despite these remaining challenges, the findings offer valuable guidance for future planetary defense efforts. The research demonstrates that the direction of a nuclear blast is not simply a minor detail. It can substantially change how effectively an asteroid is redirected.

"Our study indicates how important it is to aim carefully," Moore remarked. "Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.".

It has been revealed that the upcoming simulation tools could eventually help mission planners identify the most effective way to deflect a threatening asteroid. In principle, researchers could enter detailed information about its shape, then calculate the ideal explosive strength, distance, and direction needed to move it away from Earth.

Turning those calculations into a real mission would still be extremely difficult.

For one thing, the software requires reasonably accurate information about the asteroid's shape from every direction. If an asteroid were discovered on a collision course with Earth, there might not be enough time to gather the necessary observations.

Another challenge would be delivering and positioning a nuclear device at precisely the right location relative to an asteroid traveling through space. Even if scientists could identify the ideal blast configuration, executing it would require extraordinary precision.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, the improved simulations could eliminate much of the uncertainty surrounding one possible method of asteroid defense. By better understanding how nuclear X-rays interact with the complex surfaces of real asteroids, scientists are moving closer to predicting which strategies would work best.

For Moore, that progress is an encouraging step toward ensuring humanity has a better chance of preventing a catastrophic asteroid impact.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Another 3-2 win in Spain brings the lure of a golden new hyper-future – but it did not pan out that way last time.
  • In a recent development, I may have the body of a weak and feeble German, but I have the heart and stomach of a manager of England.
  • The words, there, of Thomas Tuchel, England’s Faerie King, speaking to TalkSport shortly after the glorious 3-2 defeat of the Spanish possession armada at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Another 3-2 win in Spain brings the lure of a golden new hyper-future – but it did not pan out that way last time.

In a recent development, I may have the body of a weak and feeble German, but I have the heart and stomach of a manager of England. And I think it foul scorn that Spain should dare to invade the borders of my realm. Or, for that matter, any one of 24 qualified teams for Euro 2028, because at the end of the day there are no easy games at this level, I’ve always mentioned that.

The words, there, of Thomas Tuchel, England’s Faerie King, speaking to TalkSport shortly after the glorious 3-2 defeat of the Spanish possession armada at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

OK, Tuchel didn’t technically say any of this. He was instead wry and spiky. He made a joke about people moaning about his team on the radio, which just goes to show he’s a good lad and one of us (disclaimer: when he wins). But this is England. And beating Spain can do some strange things to you.

Not just because Spain are the defining team of the past 20 years, six-time international trophy winners and current world and European champions. But because Spanish football culture is the global template for tone, texture and tactics, the ultimate source of the Football Association’s slightly dog‑eared footballing blueprint.

Sources indicate that beating Spain is like beating your super-smart but slightly controlling younger brother. It’s getting one over on that other way of playing, punitive high technique, death by possession, patience over urgency. Even better, Tuchel’s team did so in Madrid with a performance based around the hard‑running physicality that English football sees as part of its deep sporting soul.

Sources indicate that as such it will be tempting to see this Nations League victory as a springboard, a Rubicon crossed, a shattering of the Iberian ceiling. With some justification; England have the talent to win a home European Championship two years from now. But it feels just a little bit easier to visualise now.

In a recent development, there was something new in seeing Spain not just outmuscled but outplayed in the first half, reduced to whinging about fouls, unable to take the ball away. Not only because England’s pressing was smart and relentless but because of the players’ ability to keep possession in tight spaces.

Recent findings suggest that it is also true that a quick glance back at recent history tells us exactly how much of a golden dawn a win such as this can be. Which is: zero, zilch, nothing. No golden dawn at all.

In reality there are no Rubicon moments, no decisive levellings-up, only staging posts and warning signs, even in victory. This is the most important point about a night such as this. It won’t tell you where you’ll end up. But it may tell you how to keep heading the right way, if you’re ready to learn from recent history.

Sources indicate that as it happens, recent history is in the room with us right now, clearing its throat, rattling its chains, trying to shift the Ouija-board dial. Here is an interesting fact. Spain have only twice conceded three goals at home in a competitive men’s international. The second time was on Sunday night, when England won 3-2 in Madrid after going 3-0 up. And the first time was 15 October 2018 when England beat Spain 3-2 in Seville after going 3-0 up.

According to recent reports, the parallels between those games are numerically improbable. At the time of win No 1 Gareth Southgate had been in permanent charge for 684 days and one narrow World Cup semi-final defeat. Spain was his 29th game. At the time of win No 2 Tuchel had been in charge for 683 days and another narrow World Cup semi-final defeat. Spain was Tuchel’s 28th game.

Sources indicate that that Southgate moment was greeted with understandable optimism. You know the kind of language used because it’s out here now, too. New dawns. Statement victories. Rise of a Golden Generation. Not just a benchmark but a springboard as well, an astonishing feat of carpentry if true.

Industry observers note that so was it that? Answer: no. In fact Seville 2018 was arguably the moment Southgate-ism reached a stylistic ceiling. England played a fast-paced game of counterattack that night. The team was an attacking mix, a midfield of Winks‑Barkley‑Dier, with Sterling‑Kane‑Rashford in front. England scored 27 goals in six games the following autumn, starting most with a back four and a double pivot, ending 2019 with a 6-0, a 7-0 and a 4-0. This felt like something latest.

It has been revealed that the Covid break pretty much killed that mini-era. Or rather, it was allowed to kill it, because coaches have choices too. England went 42 weeks without a game. By November 2020 they were losing 2-0 in Belgium with a back five and a deep defensive midfield.

According to recent reports, the Euros had already been postponed for a year. In the summer of 2021 England started the final against Italy with another back five plus Declan Rice and Kalvin Phillips, and congealed into a kind of footballing rice pudding as the game reached its crisis point.

Here is an unprovable counterfactual. If football had rolled on, if England had not had an empty year to look down and get scared, they might have retained enough momentum to go harder against Italy in that final and win it.

Sources indicate that but then, the Southgate era was gruelling for many of those players. There is a separate study to be made of the way so many key early Garethistas disappeared or entered a slow decline. That October 2018 team turned out to be a pop‑up thing of shifting parts, evidence of the complex, zigzagging nature of team building.

According to recent reports, the would-be golden generation included Ben Chilwell, Eric Dier, Joe Gomez, Ross Barkley, Harry Winks and Marcus Rashford. Nathaniel Chalobah made his only appearance as a sub in added time, and still has the second-shortest England career, after Martin Kelly.

Rather than a golden dawn of ultimate glory, England entered a more talent-appropriate era of losing late-stage games against good opponents. If anything the Spain victory added to the ambient pressure around those tournaments, helping to create the sense it is now unthinkable for England to lose, because we have an image of them as winners, and English winning is the best winning, the only real winning.

It has been revealed that the lesson remains the same now, the need to avoid both portents of doom and the lure of a golden latest hyper-future. In this sense Tuchel is encouragingly restless both in defeat and victory. Even his new-season touchline look – tailored, sombre, all black – has an agreeably priestly, hair‑shirt energy; less Elizabeth I, author of the introductory quote above, more Martin Luther on his way to a business meeting in an out‑of‑town spa hotel.

Tuchel’s best quality is his obsession with analysis and objectivity. On Sunday night he was already talking about the need to improve. This can be an obstacle at times (see: process-based Argentina substitutes). But it is also a rejection of complacency, ornament, frippery. This England are better than their 2018 equivalent. That team had seven players from Leicester and Arsenal. This one has key parts from Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich, including the current Ballon d’Or winner and a £300m midfield tripod.

It has been revealed that the balance of the attack in Madrid was good, not just the most seductively talented players but the best parts for the plan. Anthony Gordon is an interesting figure in this respect, an intelligent, culturally adaptable, tactically aware footballer, whose game is nonetheless basically running up and down. Elite teams seem to have a place for this role now. Flank-scurry energy node. Right-sided gallop unit. Lewis Hall was also very good again. Any team looks better with a genuine left‑footed full-back, like hanging a picture straight on the wall.

According to recent reports, mainly what Tuchel did in Spain was to select a team with no indulgences, full commitment to a tailored gameplan, no celebrity passengers. And that style is not fixed. See also: Trent Alexander-Arnold against Croatia, and some excellent passes against a deep block even on a middling night. Stick that behind your ear as well, Thomas.

It has been revealed that teams are hugely complex things. Tuchel had to get to know his players. The idea you can simply bolt on an elite manager and expect instant progress was always a bit silly. No dips or lulls, no adaptation. This might work if you come from the same cultural system. But plonking on a brain from someone else’s body is still a way of looking for shortcuts, the managerial equivalent of sticking it in the mixer and hoping for the best. There you go. Give us a final fix on 75 years of inherited domestic culture.

Industry observers note that tuchel is now a little further along with all this. He even did the backs-to-the-wall thing better, waiting to the last moment to press the defensive emergency button, the sight of Dan Burn rumbling out a signal to both teams that this really is the end of the night, like turning on all the lights and getting the DJ to play Don’t Look Back in Anger.

Max Dowman (pictured) became England Under-21s’ youngest-ever goalscorer by grabbing the late winner in a 3-2 friendly victory over France at Ashton Gate.

Recent findings suggest that lee Carsley’s side made a lightning start as Tottenham's Mikey Moore gave England an early lead on his first under-21s start. Divin Mubama doubled their lead with a header as Ethan Nwaneri set up both of the hosts' first-half goals.

Recent findings suggest that the Young Lions looked comfortable but Tommy Setford allowed France to pull a goal back after he let Giovani Versini’s cross slip through his fingers. The French winger equalised in style moments later, scoring with a shot from distance.

Industry observers note that carsley had handed a first start to promising Arsenal youngster Dowman and he proved to be the hero, tapping in from Harrison Armstrong's pass to give England the win at only 16 years old. Press Association.

Industry observers note that sunday night was a wonderful game. It was England’s most complete performance under Tuchel. But the lesson hasn’t changed. Trust the process, not the results. Keep doing the ruthless, adaptive things that got you there. England will at some point have to beat the best. And the Nations League is a very useful tool. Win it next summer and taking that final step starts to look a whole lot less of an Arthurian fever dream.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.
  • “We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The University of Connecticut won its fifth men’s basketball national title with a 76-59 victory over San Diego State University on Monday night at NRG Stadium in Houston.

Senior guard Tristen Newton led UConn (31-8) with 19 points and 10 rebounds while Final Four Most Outstanding Player Adama Sanogo, a junior forward, chipped in with 17 points and 10 rebounds.

“We weren’t ranked going into the year so we had the chip on our shoulder,” UConn head coach Dan Hurley told game broadcaster CBS. “We knew the level that we could play at, even through those dark times,” he added, referencing the team’s six losses in eight games during the regular season.

He stated going into the tournament his group had confidence garnered during the season.

“And when you have the type of leaders like Andre Jackson (game-high six assists Monday) and Adama Sanogo, they kept this team together, got us back on track and we knew we were the best team in the tournament going in and we just had to play to our level,” he added.

San Diego State (32-7) was topped by Keshad Johnson who had 14 points.

In a recent development, UConn trailed very early but San Diego State was undone by an 11-minute, eight-second stretch in which they scored just five free throws and missed 12 consecutive shots from the field. The Huskies went from down 10-6 to up 36-24 at halftime.

The Aztecs made a run midway through the second half and narrowed the deficit to five at 60-55 with 5:19 to play but the Huskies scored the next nine to take a comfortable lead into the final two minutes.

Industry observers note that “We battled. Battled back to five in the second half, but gave them too much separation,” San Diego State coach Brian Dutcher stated. “We had to be at our best. We weren’t at our best. A lot had to do with UConn.”.

Senior guard Adam Seiko told reporters they gave themselves a chance with their second half comeback but UConn “just made a little bit more plays” at the end.

It has been revealed that “They have a lot of weapons. They were pretty good,” said Matt Bradley, also a senior guard. “To beat them, we had to make shots. I shot poorly. And you had to have a really good game to beat those dudes on the offensive end.”.

UConn won each of its six tournament games by at least 10 points, with its closest game being a 13-point win over the University of Miami in the national semifinals.

“I just want to thank my teammates, my coaches who believed in me. If it were not for them I would not be here right now,” Sanogo told CBS.

Jordan Hawkins, who scored 16 points for UConn, talked about winning the crown one day after his cousin, Angel Reese of Louisiana State University, won the women’s title.

“I mean it’s absolutely amazing that we both get this opportunity and I mean the family reunion is going to be great so that’s all I know,” he mentioned.

According to recent reports, UConn enters rarefied air as only the sixth team to win five NCAA men’s basketball championships, joining UCLA (11), Kentucky (eight), North Carolina (six), Duke (five) and Indiana (five). All of UConn’s titles have come since 1999 with the most recent before Monday occurring in 2014.

UConn’s women’s teams have won 11 basketball national titles.

CNN’s Steve Almasy and Issy Ronald contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gareth Bale (left) and Cristiano Ronaldo spent five trophy-laden years together at Real Madrid.

Portugal are just one match into life after Cristiano Ronaldo, a footballing titan whose 23-year international career transformed the game in his homeland.

On Tuesday, they visit Wales, who are nearly four years into a similar adjustment after the retirement of their own icon, Gareth Bale.

History might suggest these two teams belong to different echelons of the sport. But in terms of individual players defining entire nations, Wales and Portugal share a profound connection.

Their records only tell half the story. Ronaldo and Bale scored more goals and won more caps than any other man to represent Portugal or Wales. In Ronaldo's case, more than any other man in the world.

What the two represented for their respective countries went beyond their remarkable statistics, though.

Ronaldo led Portugal to their first title at Euro 2016, beating Bale's Wales in a semi-final and ending a momentous Welsh journey in what was their first appearance at a major tournament for 58 years.

Both players gave their countries countless memorable moments, and not only on the international stage.

Former Real Madrid team-mates, Ronaldo and Bale won four and five Champions Leagues respectively, a combined five La Liga titles and a plethora of other team and individual accolades.

Whenever they held trophies aloft, you could bet they would be carrying, or often wearing, the national flags of Portugal and Wales â global ambassadors.

"You're losing an icon of the national team," notes Wales captain Ben Davies, Bale's former team-mate and part of the Welsh defence which faced Ronaldo in what proved to be his final international appearance two months ago.

Sources indicate that "But it's an opportunity for other players to stand up and try to take that limelight. We've had boys who've really stepped up in that time after we lost probably Wales' greatest player.

"Ronaldo's a big loss but football moves on.".

Wales without injured Williams for Portugal game.

What Wales need to stay in Nations League top tier.

As secure as their legendary status might be, there are telling differences between the two.

When Bale unveiled his retirement aged 33 in January 2023, he did so because he acknowledged his once otherworldly powers were fading and he felt Wales needed to initiative for the future.

Reserved by nature, Bale could not avoid an outpouring of adulation, but he tried to depart as quietly as he could.

By contrast, Ronaldo's exit earlier this month was messy, acrimonious and, according to some, long overdue for the 41-year-old.

He walked out of a Portugal camp in September after being told he would not start a Nations League match against Denmark, resulting in a Â£215 fine and 30-day suspension.

Without knowing beforehand that the Wales game earlier that month would be his last, Ronaldo did not get the send-off he would have wanted.

"I'm grateful that we got to see the longevity of a true great who's had one of the biggest impacts in football," indicates Wales head coach Craig Bellamy.

In a recent development, "He's left a mark on football that will live forever. I'm grateful I got to see him and I'm grateful I got to coach against him.".

Six tournaments, 11 goals - Ronaldo's World Cup legacy.

Glittering and record-breaking as Ronaldo's international career undoubtedly was, the final few years were somewhat strained.

At this summer's World Cup and other recent tournaments, his star was clearly on the wane, prompting some to question whether Portugal might be better off without him.

Some of their underwhelming performances with Ronaldo leading the attack may have backed up that view, but supporters of the five-time Ballon d'Or winner could point to Portugal's first game since his retirement â Saturday's 4-1 home defeat by Denmark â as a riposte.

"You were all having a go at him for playing and then as soon as he retires then suddenly it's all hell breaks loose," Bellamy adds.

Sources indicate that "He is one of the best players that has ever played the game. We are all going to miss him.

Industry observers note that "Portugal will be completely fine. Portugal are able to leave players who cost Â£80m to Â£100m out of their squad. They can pick 30, 40 players and be ridiculous. Before that you had Figo, you had Rui Costa, before that you had Eusebio.

"The game will move on, but I always feel we should celebrate him.".

Portugal great Ronaldo retires from international duty.

'Bale departs - the day Wales dreaded'.

No-one can replace Bale - but Wilson's giving it a go.

Bellamy makes an important point, highlighting arguably the biggest distinction between Portugal's prospects after Ronaldo's retirement and the task Wales have faced since Bale's departure.

Portugal's squad is among the best in the world, littered with world-class talent in every position, a true embarrassment of riches. As Bellamy indicates, they will be fine.

The current Wales squad, meanwhile, features four League One players and one on loan in the National League.

The two teams are in the same Nations League group but worlds apart.

While Bale was part of a wider golden generation, the fact that Wales have always had to rely on thinner resources than their rivals only added to the sense of wonder that they could produce this phenomenon.

The likes of Harry Wilson have taken their game to latest levels since Bale's retirement but, as the Leeds United playmaker himself said earlier this year, nobody can replace Wales' greatest.

Industry observers note that nobody will claim to be able to replace Ronaldo either. In Portugal, he has an almost religious following.

Recent findings suggest that in pure footballing terms, though, they have more than enough to fill the void. Four of this year's Ballon d'Or nominees were Portuguese.

The reigning Nations League champions travel to Cardiff on Tuesday shorn of an all-time great but still blessed with a galaxy of stars.

According to recent reports, "Does it [Ronaldo's retirement] change how we approach the game? It doesn't, because it's just the level of quality you're up against," Bellamy claims.

"They still have about 15 Champions League winners in the squad.

"They were fine before him, then they had a brilliant moment with him, and they'll be brilliant after it as well.".

Dreaming of a bright and shiny future filled with personal jet packs, levitating autos, and automated gadgets straight out of "The Jetsons?" "In Metropia, a gigantic city in an alternate future as seen from 1939, private eye Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell) is drawn into a case involving aliens, murder, and a multimedia starlet named Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson)," states the official synopsis.

Netflix Films and Skydance Animation's "Ray Gunn" is a stylistic pastiche of classic film noir tropes populated by down-and-out detectives and femme fatales living in the inspiring air of technological optimism viewed through a pre-war America lens.

Think "The Fifth Element" meets "Who Framed Roger Rabbit?" and "The Maltese Falcon," and you’re going to be close to this sci-fi whodunnit's vibe, which is intended for more mature audiences and rated PG.

In a recent development, this energetic new preview is locked and loaded with dazzling visuals by Cinesite, freaky creatures, streamlined flying cars, and a blistering pace. And if you listen very closely, The B-52s' "Planet Claire" can be heard playing in the background, which is one of the touchstones that inspired Bird to begin his 36-year journey to bring "Ray Gunn" to life. Was it worth the wait? We'll have to find out.

It has been revealed that also starring the vocal talents of Tom Waits, Bobby Cannavale, Alan Tudyk, Matt Berry, and Michelle Rodriguez, "Ray Gunn" opens in select theaters and 70mm screenings Dec. 4. After that, it lands on Netflix on Dec. 18... a date you might want to circle on your calendar, as that’s also the release slot for "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Dune: Part 3.".

Recent findings suggest that it's going to be a busy day for sci-fi fans. "Strap in, buster!".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An extraordinary collection of fossils in central Colombia is revealing a surprising chapter in Earth's evolutionary history.
  • Industry observers note that scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this unusual pattern while studying fossils from Colombia's Paja Formation.
  • Drawing on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a upcoming concept called a "Biotic Inflection." The term describes an evolutionary turning point when older groups nearing extinction coexist with newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An extraordinary collection of fossils in central Colombia is revealing a surprising chapter in Earth's evolutionary history. Researchers have uncovered evidence of a time when ancient animal groups that were approaching extinction lived alongside newer groups that would eventually flourish. The discovery suggests that major evolutionary transitions can occur without the widespread destruction associated with mass extinctions.

Industry observers note that scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this unusual pattern while studying fossils from Colombia's Paja Formation. The ancient marine ecosystem preserves an exceptional mixture of surviving Jurassic lineages and emerging Cretaceous groups, offering a rare glimpse into a period of profound biological change.

Drawing on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a upcoming concept called a "Biotic Inflection." The term describes an evolutionary turning point when older groups nearing extinction coexist with newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify.

A Perfect Storm for Ancient Ocean Biodiversity.

The researchers believe an unusual combination of environmental conditions helped make this remarkable coexistence possible. Warm greenhouse temperatures, elevated sea levels, and coastal waters rich in nutrients may have supported an unusually diverse range of marine life.

It has been revealed that another important factor was the emergence of new ocean connections between the eastern Pacific and the early Atlantic through the region that is now Colombia. Together, these conditions likely created opportunities for different groups of animals to thrive within the same ecosystem. Many of these environmental influences continue to shape biodiversity around the world today.

According to recent reports, "The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a 'perfect storm' of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish," Larsson stated.

A Lost World of Giant Marine Reptiles and Predators.

The evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia. This fossil-rich region has preserved an astonishing variety of prehistoric marine animals, providing scientists with an unusually detailed picture of an ancient ocean ecosystem. Most of the fossils collected from the formation are housed at the CIP.

According to recent reports, "This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others," Cortés explained. "Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date.".

According to recent reports, in a previous study, the researchers reconstructed the feeding relationships among animals in the Paja Biota. Their analysis revealed an exceptionally intricate food web, with an unusually large variety of apex predators occupying the highest levels of the ecosystem.

This remarkable complexity makes the Paja Formation especially valuable for investigating how ecosystems change as older evolutionary groups decline and new ones become established.

Could This Discovery Change How Scientists Understand Evolution?

Sources indicate that the proposed Biotic Inflection offers a potentially important fresh way to understand major changes in Earth's biodiversity. Rather than being driven by a mass extinction, some evolutionary transitions may involve periods of extraordinary diversity, when declining lineages and emerging groups coexist.

Recent findings suggest that however, the researchers emphasize that more evidence is needed to establish how common this pattern may have been. Additional fossil discoveries, more accurate estimates of fossil ages, and comparisons with geological formations in other parts of the world will help determine whether similar transitions occurred elsewhere in Earth's history.

Industry observers note that "I think we've discovered a upcoming model of global biodiversity change. Now we'll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth's history and how we can quantify its impacts," Larsson stated.

Recent findings suggest that the research received funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, the Anders Foundation, the 1923 Fund, Gregory D. and Jennifer Walston Johnson, the Fonds de recherche Nature et technologies Québec, and the McGill Biology Department Writing-Year Award 2024-2025.

Mauricio Pochettino says he would tell Pep Guardiola to take the United States job if the former Manchester City manager was offered it.

Pochettino, 54, is leaving his role as the US men's team head coach to become Manchester United's latest manager from 18 November, after signing a two-and-a-half-year contract until June 2029.

He takes charge of his final game with the US on Tuesday when they face Haiti in the second leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals in Cincinnati, Ohio.

Guardiola, 55, is taking a one-year sabbatical after stepping down as City boss in May.

Reports have suggested Guardiola could be a contender to succeed Pochettino in the US, although there has been no formal contact between the Spaniard and the United States Soccer Federation.

Pochettino told reporters on Monday his advice to Guardiola would be to take the role, "because it's a perfect moment to arrive at the federation.".

The Argentine added: "Everything is on the right path, in the right direction.

According to recent reports, "Of course, take it. Of course, you are going to find really good players, good people - the players can fit his style.".

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino is replacing Michael Carrick at United. Carrick was sacked as head coach last week with the club in the relegation zone in 18th place.

His long-time assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeping coach Toni Jimenez and athletic coach, 31-year-old son Sebastiano Pochettino, arrived in England following the US's 6-0 first-leg victory over Haiti in Miami last weekend.

Pochettino's first test back in the Premier League is an away trip to Anfield to face fourth-placed Liverpool on Sunday.

"They are in advance, they are preparing all there, because Wednesday when we will arrive, it is going to be non-stop," he said.

It comes after Spain's head coach Luis de la Fuente insisted there was no racism in Spain or in Spanish football before their Nations League meeting with England in Madrid on Sunday.
